events.title: The revocation of the Edict of Nantes
events.shortBlurb: By the Edict of Fontainebleau Louis XIV revoked the toleration of 1598, silenced the Reformed churches, and scattered the Huguenots across the world…
body: For fourscore and seven years the Edict of Nantes, granted by Henry IV in 1598, had given the Reformed of France a measured toleration. Under Louis XIV the measure was steadily withdrawn, church by church and office by office, until on 18 October 1685 the king signed at Fontainebleau the edict that revoked his grandfather's grant altogether.

Public worship was forbidden to the Protestants, their churches razed, their ministers ordered from the realm within fifteen days; parents were commanded to have their children baptized and schooled as Catholics; and emigration was banned for men on pain of the galleys, for women of prison.

The blow was applauded in France — Vauban and Saint-Simon were nearly alone in deploring it — yet it scattered a multitude: Vauban reckoned a hundred thousand Frenchmen lost to the kingdom, with sixty million livres, nine thousand sailors, and the best of her officers gone to her enemies. The proscribed worship lived on in secret assemblies "in the desert," and flared into the Camisard war of the Cévennes in 1702.
